prompt: A buyer gives you a one-word answer after your opening question. Your instinct is to:

options.text: Ask another question immediately to keep momentum
Offer more context about your product to fill the gap
Acknowledge what they said and bridge to your next point
Reflect their last word or phrase back as a question
Name the emotion behind their short answer and hold silence

prompt: Mid-meeting, a buyer says: 'We've tried this before and it didn't work.' You:

options.text: Immediately explain why this time will be different
Apologise and offer a discount to rebuild goodwill
Ask them to tell you more about what happened
Reflect back: 'Didn't work?' and wait
Name the feeling: 'It sounds like that experience left you cautious about committing again.'

prompt: There is a 7-second silence after you ask a key discovery question. You:

options.text: Fill the silence quickly with a clarifying follow-up question, just to keep things moving
Rephrase the question in a different way in case they didn't quite understand it
Wait up to 5 seconds after asking, then gently prompt them if nothing comes
Hold the silence, since they are still processing it and will speak when ready
Summarise what you've heard so far to give them something to react to

prompt: You misread a buyer's emotion. They say, 'I'm not worried; I'm frustrated.' You:

options.text: Apologise and move on: 'Sorry, my mistake, let's keep going and not dwell on it.'
Defend your original read: 'I hear you, but you still seem worried to me from where I'm sitting.'
Acknowledge the correction: 'Thanks for that, tell me more about what's actually driving it.'
Name the emotion more precisely: 'It sounds like I missed that; it's more frustration than worry.'
Pivot to a solution: 'Let's talk about how we fix the frustration you're feeling.'

prompt: A buyer says very little but their body language is tense. You prioritise:

options.text: Pushing straight through your agenda, assuming they're just busy today
Asking them a direct question: 'Is everything okay right now?'
Slowing your pace down and asking an open, calibrated question
Naming what you observe: 'There's a lot on your plate.'
Acknowledging the visible tension and offering to reschedule the call

prompt: After a strong discovery session, a buyer goes cold and stops responding. You:

options.text: Send a quick 'just checking in' follow-up email to keep the conversation open for now
Call them directly and walk back through your proposal in more detail
Send a short, low-pressure email asking whether their priorities have shifted since you last spoke
Acknowledge that their attention seems to have shifted and offer to pause
Wait a couple of weeks before reaching out to them again

prompt: A client is venting about a difficult internal situation that has nothing to do with your proposal. You:

options.text: Listen politely for a moment, then redirect the conversation back to your agenda
Offer sympathy by saying 'I'm sorry to hear that' and pause for a moment
Ask a thoughtful question that connects their situation back to your proposed solution
Fully listen to what they're saying, then reflect back what you heard before moving on
Name what they're feeling and invite them to say more before pivoting

prompt: You sense a buyer is holding back — they're agreeable but not engaged. You:

options.text: Present more compelling data or examples in an effort to re-engage them again
Ask them directly whether they're interested in moving forward with the proposal right now
Ask an open question: 'What's most important to you as you think this through?'
Name what you notice: 'It seems like something hasn't quite landed yet.'
Give them space by pushing less and letting them come to you naturally

prompt: A major deal falls apart at the last minute due to internal politics you didn't see. Your immediate response is:

options.text: Review what data you could have presented differently
Analyse the relationship dynamics — who had influence you didn't map?
Follow up with the buyer to understand what changed
Accept it as part of the game and move to the next deal
Ask the buyer directly what the real reason was

prompt: A client gives you positive feedback to your face but doesn't return calls. You interpret this as:

options.text: They're genuinely interested in what you're offering but simply pulled in other directions
They were simply being polite, and the deal is most likely already dead
A sign of something unspoken: 'There's more going on behind the scenes than they're letting on.'
A signal to send even more proof points and case studies to build the case
A sign that something has shifted internally that hasn't been named yet

prompt: In a group pitch, one stakeholder keeps interrupting with objections while others stay silent. You:

options.text: Address the loud objector head-on right away to try to neutralise their resistance
Pause the conversation for a moment and directly ask the quieter stakeholders what they think
Continue delivering your pitch as planned and handle any objections once you're finished
Acknowledge the objector's concern directly, then open the floor to the rest of the room
Name the dynamic in the room and invite other perspectives to surface

prompt: A long-term client suddenly reduces their spend with no explanation. Your first move is:

options.text: Send over a revised proposal with more competitive pricing to win them back
Request a meeting to walk them through some new campaign options and ideas
Call them directly and ask if anything has changed on their end recently
Name what you're sensing and ask directly what's changed on their end
Speak to your manager first to get their read before reaching out to the client

prompt: A procurement officer says: 'Match this rate or the budget moves to your competitor.' You:

options.text: Match the rate straight away without pushback in order to protect the long-term relationship
Defend your rate card firmly using audience numbers and reach data to back it up
Acknowledge the pressure they're under and ask what outcome they're really trying to optimise for
Name the pressure they're under and ask what success looks like for them
Ask for some time to consult your manager before you give them a response

prompt: A buyer says 'We don't have budget' and then goes silent. You:

options.text: Offer them a lower-cost option right away to keep the conversation moving forward
Ask them directly when their budget cycle is expected to reset next
Reflect it back: 'No budget?' and then hold the silence to see what comes next
Ask: 'What did the budget situation look like before this conversation started?'
Say: 'Here's the ROI case that I believe justifies the spend' and walk them through it

prompt: Mid-pitch, a senior stakeholder says 'I've heard all this before.' You:

options.text: Say: 'Let's skip ahead to the part that matters most to you.'
Acknowledge it honestly and ask what would make this worth their time
Defend your approach by explaining how it's different from what competitors offer
Ask them directly: 'What didn't land for you last time we talked?'
Wrap up efficiently and follow up afterward with a proposal tailored to them

prompt: An agency contact says: 'Your competitor is offering CPC guarantees and post-click attribution. Can you match it?' You:

options.text: Say: 'Let's lock this in now and work out the details afterward.'
Explain directly: 'CPC guarantees often hide misleading metrics that don't tell the full story.'
Acknowledge the ask and check whether attribution visibility is really the driver here
Ask them directly what they'd actually do with the attribution data if they had it
Offer them a performance bonus structure instead as a fair middle-ground compromise

prompt: You've used the phrase 'I completely understand' three times in a difficult meeting. You:

options.text: Don't notice — it's a natural empathy signal
Notice but it's better than silence
Recognise it's a filler — you need to ask a better question instead
Stop using it and replace it with a calibrated question
Use it once more, then pivot to closing

prompt: A client says 'The last campaign didn't move the needle — we need guarantees to proceed.' You:

options.text: Promise strong results upfront in order to close the deal as quickly as possible
Ask them directly what 'moving the needle' actually means to them specifically
Say: 'Here's a new campaign structure built with much stronger targeting this time.'
Acknowledge that the previous investment left them needing more certainty before committing again
Say: 'Here's a case study from a similar client that shows comparable results.'

prompt: You have 2 minutes to introduce your solution in a first meeting. You start with:

options.text: Your company's overall reach and detailed audience data
Say: 'Here's what makes our product different from everything else out there.'
Ask them: 'What's the biggest challenge you're facing with this right now?'
A brief story about a client who faced a similar situation
A specific, quote-based client story

prompt: A sceptical CMO asks 'Why should I choose you over your competitor?' You respond with:

options.text: Walk them through it directly: 'Here's what the actual numbers show: reach, CPM, and audience data from your current media kit for this campaign.'
Say directly: 'Here are your top three differentiators, and each one is backed by a solid proof point we can show you right now.'
A client success story that lets someone else make your case for you, complete with a specific and clearly measurable outcome for them
A short story that draws them into the moment, the place, the stakes, what you did, ending on the client's own words
A question back that turns the pressure right around on them: 'What would success actually look like for you in this space right now?'

prompt: You want to make a campaign result memorable in a presentation. You present it as:

options.text: 'We reached 450,000 people in the metro area'
'We filled ANZ Stadium five times over in a single breakfast shift'
'Our campaign delivered a 28% lift in sales'
'Our results exceeded industry benchmarks by 2.3x'
A before-and-after story ending with a client quote about the impact

prompt: Your agency contact is putting multiple publisher options in front of the client and will make the recommendation. You help your proposal stand out by:

options.text: Including all the data they might need to reference
Briefing them on your top three product features
Giving them a clear ROI argument they can use in the comparison
Arming them with one short, vivid story they can retell confidently
Following up with a summary email after the meeting

prompt: A client is hesitating because the previous publisher/vendor 'let them down.' You address this by:

options.text: Say directly: 'Here's exactly how our accountability processes and reporting will keep you informed every step of the way.'
Offer them a clear performance-based pricing model, and say: 'You'll only pay us based on the results we actually deliver.'
Share a detailed testimonial from a client who was in a very similar situation before working with us
Telling a specific story of how you helped a client in a similar post-disappointment situation
Acknowledge their concern directly, then move the conversation toward your product's core strengths and what sets it apart

prompt: In your story, the client is the hero. This means:

options.text: You emphasise how great your product performed for them throughout the campaign
You focus mainly on your team's strategic thinking and flawless execution behind the scenes
You centre the story on the client's problem and their relief when it was solved
You split the credit equally between your company and the client for the win
You lead with the data that proves the outcome

prompt: When a client stops responding to your outreach, your gut says:

options.text: You read it as them just being busy, so you keep following up on a regular schedule
Your instinct says something changed internally on their end, so you dig in to find out what before assuming anything
Your gut says the deal is dead, so you move on and focus your energy elsewhere
Name what you sense: 'It feels like the timing may have shifted; I want to respect that.'
You feel it's time to cut your losses, so you send a breakup email to try to re-engage them one last time

prompt: You notice a five-second silence on a video call right after you've asked for the business. You:

options.text: Fill it immediately with reassurance
Repeat your ask in a different way
Hold the silence — they're processing
Ask if they have any final questions
Summarise your key points again

prompt: A client is calm and agreeable but you sense the deal isn't moving. You:

options.text: Take their positivity at face value and move the conversation forward as planned
Ask them directly: 'What does your decision-making timeline actually look like from here?'
Name what you're sensing and ask directly if you're reading the situation right
Send over a more detailed proposal that addresses any concerns they haven't voiced yet
Ask their assistant directly: 'Is there anything going on I should know about?'

prompt: The real reason a buyer says no is almost always:

options.text: Price — buyers are budget-constrained
Timing — the market isn't right
Risk — they fear looking bad if the campaign underperforms
Product — your offering doesn't fit their needs
Competition — a competitor made a better offer

prompt: When a buyer pushes back hard on your proposal, your first physical instinct is:

options.text: To defend your position — you believe in what you're selling
To apologise and offer a concession
To breathe, pause, and ask a question
To ask what specifically isn't working for them
To acknowledge the pushback and invite them to say more

prompt: The most important thing to understand about a buyer before you pitch is:

options.text: Their overall budget range for this specific campaign
Their preferred media channels and formats for this
Their specific KPIs and how they measure success
What they personally fear happening if it fails
Their working relationship with their previous media agency

prompt: Clients don't buy media plans. They buy:

options.text: Reach and frequency
Cost efficiency
Innovation and differentiation
Certainty and relief — the confidence they won't be embarrassed by this decision
Data-backed justification for their spend

prompt: EQ Identity EQ1

options.text: When a client is emotional, my strength is staying calm and not reacting
My strength is using their emotion as information to guide my next move
My strength is noticing the emotion before they've said anything
My strength is naming the emotion out loud — even when it's uncomfortable

prompt: EQ Identity EQ2

options.text: Under pressure I stay logical and don't let feelings cloud my judgement
Under pressure I look for the emotional lever the other person hasn't used yet
Under pressure I watch and wait — reading the room before I act
Under pressure I call out what's really happening — even if it's awkward

prompt: EQ Identity EQ3

options.text: After a difficult meeting I debrief by reviewing what logic/data I used
After a difficult meeting I debrief by thinking about what emotional leverage I did or didn't use
After a difficult meeting I replay what I noticed — body language, silence, energy
After a difficult meeting I think about whether I named the hard thing or avoided it
